chapter_title: Scrum Events: The Heartbeat of an Agile Project
chapter_summary:
Scrum isn't just a set of roles and artifacts; it's a dynamic framework driven by a series of prescribed events. These events are the heartbeat of an agile project, providing regular opportunities for inspection and adaptation, ensuring transparency, and keeping the team aligned and focused. Each event is time-boxed, meaning it has a maximum duration, ensuring that time is used effectively and preventing unnecessary overhead. Let's dive into the five core Scrum events, starting with the overarching container: the Sprint.

The **Sprint** itself is a time-box of one month or less during which a "Done," usable, and potentially releasable product Increment is created. Sprints are consistent in duration throughout a development effort. This consistency helps create a rhythm and predictability for the Scrum Team. Once a Sprint begins, its duration is fixed, and no changes are made that would endanger the Sprint Goal. It's a mini-project within itself, with its own goal, design, development, testing, and delivery. A common mistake is to let Sprint lengths fluctuate or to extend a Sprint if the work isn't finished. This undermines predictability and the discipline of time-boxing. The Sprint provides the container for all other Scrum events.

The Sprint kicks off with **Sprint Planning**. This event is time-boxed to a maximum of eight hours for a one-month Sprint, and typically shorter for shorter Sprints. During Sprint Planning, the entire Scrum Team collaborates to define the Sprint Goal and select Product Backlog items that will be worked on during the Sprint. The Development Team determines *how* they will build the selected items and create the "Done" Increment. This involves creating the initial Sprint Backlog. Sprint Planning answers three key questions: What can be delivered in the Increment resulting from the upcoming Sprint? How will the work needed to deliver the Increment be achieved? And why is this Sprint valuable? A frequent anti-pattern is the Development Team being told what to do rather than actively participating in the commitment, or over-committing to too much work, leading to incomplete items at the Sprint's end. Effective Sprint Planning requires a well-refined Product Backlog and a realistic understanding of the Development Team's capacity.

Once the Sprint is underway, the **Daily Scrum** becomes the primary event for the Development Team to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog as necessary. This is a 15-minute time-boxed event held at the same time and place each day for the Development Team. It's an internal meeting for the Development Team, though the Scrum Master ensures it happens and the Product Owner can attend as an observer. The purpose is to optimize team collaboration and performance. The Development Team plans work for the next 24 hours. This is *not* a status report to the Scrum Master or Product Owner. A common mistake is for team members to report what they did yesterday and what they will do today without discussing impediments or how their work contributes to the Sprint Goal. Instead, it should be a quick planning meeting where the team inspects their progress, identifies any roadblocks, and collaboratively decides on the best course of action for the next day to achieve the Sprint Goal.

Midway or towards the end of the Sprint, the **Sprint Review** occurs. This event is time-boxed to a maximum of four hours for a one-month Sprint. Its purpose is to inspect the Increment and adapt the Product Backlog if needed. The Scrum Team and key stakeholders collaborate on what was done in the Sprint. The Product Owner explains what Product Backlog items have been "Done" and what has not been "Done." The Development Team discusses what went well during the Sprint, what problems it ran into, and how those problems were solved. They demonstrate the "Done" work and answer questions about the Increment. The entire group collaborates on what to do next, which might involve revising the Product Backlog. A common anti-pattern is for the Sprint Review to be a one-way presentation by the Development Team without active feedback or collaboration from stakeholders. It should be an informal, working meeting, not a formal gate or a mere demo.

Finally, the Sprint concludes with the **Sprint Retrospective**. This event is time-boxed to a maximum of three hours for a one-month Sprint. It's an opportunity for the Scrum Team to inspect itself and create a plan for improvements to be enacted during the next Sprint. The purpose is to increase quality and effectiveness. The Scrum Team discusses: What went well during the Sprint? What could be improved? What will we commit to improve in the next Sprint? The Scrum Master ensures the meeting is positive and productive. A common mistake is for retrospectives to become a "blame game" or a session where issues are raised but no concrete, actionable improvements are identified and committed to. The outcome should be at least one high-priority, actionable improvement that the Scrum Team commits to implementing in the upcoming Sprint.

These events, when executed correctly, form a continuous feedback loop, enabling the Scrum Team to continuously inspect and adapt its product and process, embodying the core principles of agility.

screens.title: Scrum Events: The Heartbeat of an Agile Project
screens.subtitle: How Sprints, Planning, Daily Scrums, Reviews, and Retrospectives keep teams inspecting, adapting, and delivering

narration.text: In Scrum, events are not optional meetings — they are the rhythm that keeps a team aligned and focused. In this lesson you will learn what each prescribed event does, why it is time-boxed, and how the five events fit inside a Sprint to create a continuous loop of inspection and adaptation. We’ll treat the Sprint as the container where a usable Increment is built, show how Sprint Planning sets a clear Sprint Goal, explain how the Daily Scrum keeps daily progress visible, and describe how the Review and Retrospective insert stakeholder feedback and team improvement into the next cycle. You will also see common anti-patterns to avoid, such as extending a Sprint, turning reviews into one-way demos, or letting retrospectives become blame sessions. For a concrete example, we’ll use a two-week Sprint scenario to show realistic time-boxes and typical attendee lists. By the end, you should be able to explain the purpose and proper time-box for each event, identify one common pitfall for each event, and describe the flow and handoffs that let a Scrum Team deliver predictable increments. How will you apply this rhythm to create better predictability on your next Sprint?

screens.title: The Sprint: a Time-boxed Container
screens.subtitle: One month or less; a fixed rhythm for creating a Done Increment

narration.text: A Sprint is the primary container for all Scrum events. It is a time-box of one month or less during which the Scrum Team creates a Done, usable, and potentially releasable product Increment. Time-box means a fixed maximum duration: once a Sprint starts its end date is set and the team must plan and deliver within that window. Practically, a Sprint behaves like a mini-project with design, development, testing, and delivery. Consistency of Sprint length across the development effort creates a predictable cadence and makes velocity meaningful. A concrete example: in a two-week Sprint the team sets a Sprint Goal and commits to the Sprint Backlog during Sprint Planning, meets daily to inspect progress, demonstrates the Increment to stakeholders near the end, and inspects the process in a Retrospective. A common misconception is that a Sprint can be extended if work is unfinished. That undermines predictability — incomplete items return to the Product Backlog and are re-prioritized. Key takeaway: a Sprint protects focus, enforces deadlines, and creates a repeating opportunity to learn about the product and the team’s delivery capability.

keyIdea.title: Sprint is a fixed mini-project
keyIdea.text: Keep Sprint length consistent; do not extend a Sprint to complete unfinished work.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › The Sprint
Definition & Properties
A Sprint is a time-box of one month or less during which a Done, usable, and potentially releasable Increment is created.
Fixed duration: once started, the Sprint end date is set.
Consistent length: keeps a predictable rhythm and meaningful velocity.
Contains all events: Planning, Daily, Review, Retrospective happen inside it.
Concrete example
Two-week Sprint: Sprint Planning (max 4 hours), Daily Scrums each day (15 min), Sprint Review (max 2 hours), Sprint Retrospective (max 1.5 hours). At the end, unfinished Product Backlog items return to the Product Backlog.
Why it matters and common mistakes
  • Protects focus and creates a measurable delivery rhythm.
  • Enables predictable inspection points for product and process.
  • Anti-pattern: extending Sprints undermines predictability and learning.
Key Takeaway

A Sprint’s fixed time-box creates a reliable cadence. Keep lengths consistent and avoid extensions to protect predictability.

screens.title: Sprint Planning: Start with a Clear Goal
screens.subtitle: Define what will be delivered and how the team will do the work

narration.text: Sprint Planning is a collaborative event where the Scrum Team defines a Sprint Goal and selects Product Backlog items to create the initial Sprint Backlog. For a one-month Sprint the meeting is time-boxed to a maximum of eight hours; for a two-week Sprint it will be shorter, often around four hours. Sprint Planning answers three questions: what can be delivered in the upcoming Increment, how will the work be achieved, and why is this Sprint valuable. Preparation matters: the Product Backlog should be refined so selections are ready for estimation and commitment. The Development Team decides how to implement selected items, breaking work down and assessing capacity. A practical two-week example: set a clear Sprint Goal, pull small, well-defined backlog items totaling the team's forecast capacity, and agree on the initial Sprint Backlog with explicit Done criteria. A common anti-pattern is telling the Development Team what to do instead of letting them commit; another is over-committing. Fixes include realistic capacity planning, honest estimation, and ensuring the Product Owner clarifies priorities in advance. The outcome is a shared commitment and a Sprint Backlog the team believes it can complete.

keyIdea.title: Three key questions
keyIdea.text: Sprint Planning answers: What will be delivered, how will we build it, and why is it valuable.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Sprint Planning
Sprint Planning steps
1. Product Owner presents priority items and the desired outcome.
2. Development Team forecasts capacity and selects items they can complete.
3. Team defines the Sprint Goal and creates the initial Sprint Backlog with tasks and Done criteria.
Example — 2-week Sprint
Time-box: ~4 hours. Activities: clarify priorities, estimate tasks, commit to a Sprint Goal that guides daily work.
Common mistakes & fixes
  • Anti-pattern: Team told what to do — fix by involving Development Team in commitment decisions.
  • Anti-pattern: Over-committing — fix by using realistic capacity and historical velocity.
  • Anti-pattern: Unrefined backlog — fix with regular backlog refinement prior to planning.
Key Takeaway

Sprint Planning creates a shared Sprint Goal and a realistic Sprint Backlog. Preparation and team ownership prevent over-commitment.

screens.title: Planning Pitfalls: What Often Goes Wrong
screens.subtitle: Common anti-patterns and how to correct them

narration.text: Sprint Planning can go wrong in predictable ways. The first anti-pattern is over-commitment: teams take on more Product Backlog items than they can complete. This often happens when estimates are optimistic or when capacity is miscalculated. The practical correction is to use historical velocity and leave contingency for unforeseen work. The second anti-pattern is the Development Team being told what to do by the Product Owner or managers. Scrum requires the Development Team to decide how they will accomplish the work; remedy this by facilitating collaborative planning and ensuring the Product Owner brings priorities rather than commands. The third is holding Planning with an unrefined backlog, forcing long guessing sessions. Fix this with routine backlog refinement so items are ready to be sized. A concrete two-week Sprint checklist: prepare refined backlog items, estimate in team sessions before planning, calculate capacity considering holidays and support duties, and draft a clear Sprint Goal. Recognizing these patterns and applying the corrective checks makes Sprint Planning efficient and realistic rather than a scheduling exercise gone wrong. Planning Pitfalls: What Often Goes Wrong means use historical data, involve the development team in commitments, and refine backlog items in advance.. In practical terms, common anti-patterns and how to correct them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Fixable planning errors
keyIdea.text: Use historical data, involve the Development Team in commitments, and refine backlog items in advance.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Planning Pitfalls
Anti-patterns
Over-commitment: choosing too much scope for the Sprint.
Being told what to do: Development Team lacks ownership of the plan.
Unrefined backlog: planning stalls while items are clarified.
Practical corrections
  • Use historical velocity and explicit capacity when forecasting.
  • Facilitate collaborative planning; Product Owner explains priorities and team chooses the plan.
  • Refine backlog items beforehand so planning focuses on choices rather than clarification.
Two-week Sprint checklist
Refined items, capacity calculation, draft Sprint Goal, task breakdown, Done criteria, acceptance by Development Team.

screens.title: Daily Scrum: 15 Minutes of Focused Planning
screens.subtitle: A short, daily inspect-and-adapt meeting for the Development Team

narration.text: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute time-boxed event held at the same time and place each day for the Development Team. Its purpose is to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog for the next 24 hours. It is not a status report to the Scrum Master or Product Owner; rather, it's the Development Team’s planning meeting. In practice, team members quickly surface progress, identify impediments, and agree on next steps. For example, a developer might say they are blocked by a missing A P I credential and the team immediately assigns someone after the meeting to unblock work. A common misconception is that each person must give a detailed account of yesterday’s work. That wastes the 15-minute time-box. The better approach is to focus on how the work aligns with the Sprint Goal and what adjustments are needed. If a complex issue arises, take it offline with only relevant people right after the Daily Scrum. The Daily Scrum optimizes collaboration and helps discover and resolve impediments early. Ask yourself: what small plan change will bring the Sprint Goal within reach in the next 24 hours?

keyIdea.title: Daily planning, not status
keyIdea.text: Keep the meeting short and planning-focused; take deeper problem-solving offline after the meeting.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Daily Scrum
Purpose & Rules
15-minute time-box for the Development Team to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog.
Held at the same time and place each day to create rhythm.
Focus on planning the next 24 hours; not a status report to managers.
Scrum Master ensures it occurs; Product Owner may attend as observer.
Example & Tip
Example: "I’m finishing the login feature; blocked on API key. I can pair with Alex after this meeting to remove the blocker."
Common mistake
Turning the Daily Scrum into lengthy technical problem-solving. Fix: schedule a short follow-up with just the needed team members.
Key Takeaway

Use the Daily Scrum to adapt the plan for the next day. Keep it short, focused, and action-oriented.

screens.title: Daily Scrum Anti-patterns and the Scrum Master Role
screens.subtitle: How the meeting can drift and how to coach it back to purpose

narration.text: Several recurring problems can reduce the effectiveness of the Daily Scrum. First, the meeting can become a status report directed at the Scrum Master or Product Owner. This removes team ownership and turns a planning meeting into passive updates. The Scrum Master’s role is to coach the Development Team to run the event themselves and to remove impediments, not to act as a manager taking notes. Second, daily discussions can veer into long problem-solving sessions that eat the 15-minute time-box. The right response is to note the issue and set a focused follow-up with only needed participants immediately after the Daily Scrum. Third, inconsistent timing or location kills rhythm; hold the meeting at the same time and place to create a reliable pattern. A practical coaching script for a Scrum Master: remind the team of the Sprint Goal, prompt them to identify impediments, and suggest offline problem-solving when the discussion deepens. A quick contrast: a productive Daily Scrum results in a short, coordinated plan for the next 24 hours; a broken Daily Scrum results in unclear next steps and stalled delivery. Which small change will you coach in your next Daily Scrum?

keyIdea.title: Coach, don't control
keyIdea.text: Scrum Masters coach the team to keep the Daily Scrum short, team-owned, and rhythmical.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Daily Scrum Coaching
Common anti-patterns
Status report to Scrum Master or Product Owner.
Long technical problem-solving during the meeting.
Irregular schedule that breaks team rhythm.
Coaching moves for Scrum Masters
  • Remind the team this is their planning meeting and prompt them to adapt the Sprint Backlog.
  • When deep discussion starts, request an offline follow-up and note the participants.
  • Keep the meeting at the same time and place to create a predictable cadence.
Quick script
"What’s our plan for the next 24 hours to reach the Sprint Goal? Who is blocked and who can help? If we need a longer dive, let’s meet right after with the necessary people."

screens.title: Sprint Review: Inspect the Increment with Stakeholders
screens.subtitle: Demonstrate Done work, gather feedback, and adapt the Product Backlog

narration.text: The Sprint Review is a working meeting where the Scrum Team and key stakeholders inspect the Increment and collaborate on what to do next. It is time-boxed to a maximum of four hours for a one-month Sprint and shorter for shorter Sprints. During the Review the Product Owner explains which Product Backlog items are Done and which are not. The Development Team demonstrates the work, discusses what went well and what problems occurred, and answers questions about the Increment. The key outcome is collaborative input that may change the Product Backlog. A common anti-pattern is turning the Review into a one-way demo where stakeholders passively watch and do not offer feedback that changes priorities. The correct approach treats the Review as an informal discussion: stakeholders interact with the Increment, test functionality, and co-create next steps with the Product Owner. An example: in a two-week Sprint the Review lasts up to two hours and ends with a list of suggested backlog changes prioritized by the Product Owner. The Sprint Review turns delivered work into learning and updated plans for the product.

keyIdea.title: Collaborative inspection
keyIdea.text: Reviews are interactive: stakeholders inspect, test, and shape the Product Backlog together with the Scrum Team.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Sprint Review
Purpose & Activities
  • Inspect the Increment and gather stakeholder feedback.
  • Product Owner explains what is Done and what is not.
  • Collaborate on what to do next, updating the Product Backlog.
Example — 2-week Sprint
Time-box: ~2 hours. Demonstrate features, collect feedback, and list Product Backlog adjustments for prioritization.
Anti-pattern & remedy
Anti-pattern: a one-way demo without stakeholder collaboration. Remedy: invite active stakeholders, ask for specific feedback, and agree on backlog updates before closing the Review.
Key Takeaway

Treat the Review as a joint inspection that leads directly to Product Backlog adaptations and informed next steps.

screens.title: Sprint Review: How to Make Stakeholder Feedback Actionable
screens.subtitle: Invite, demonstrate, and convert feedback into backlog changes

narration.text: Collecting stakeholder feedback in a Sprint Review only creates value when it becomes actionable. Start by inviting stakeholders who can provide decision-making input or technical feedback. During the Review, demonstrate the Increment in a way that allows stakeholders to try or see the feature in context. Ask open questions that surface change requests, and document suggested backlog items or edits. After the meeting the Product Owner collaborates with the Scrum Team to refine and prioritize those suggestions in the Product Backlog. A common mistake is to log feedback without clear follow-up; this leads to stakeholder frustration and lost learning. Make feedback actionable by converting each suggestion into a backlog item with acceptance criteria or a refinement note. Also avoid treating Reviews as formal gates; they are informal working sessions for adaptation. For a two-hour Review in a two-week Sprint, end the session with a prioritized list of backlog changes or experiments. Doing this ensures the Review’s learning immediately informs product direction. Sprint Review: How to Make Stakeholder Feedback Actionable means turn stakeholder feedback into prioritized product backlog items with clear acceptance criteria.. In practical terms, invite, demonstrate, and convert feedback into backlog changes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: From feedback to backlog
keyIdea.text: Turn stakeholder feedback into prioritized Product Backlog items with clear acceptance criteria.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Review → Action
Make feedback actionable
  1. Invite decision-makers who can change priorities.
  2. Demonstrate real functionality, not slides.
  3. Capture suggested changes as backlog items with acceptance details.
Avoid these mistakes
Logging feedback without owners or next steps leaves learning unused.
Treating Reviews as formal gates rather than collaborative adaptation points.
Key Takeaway

Finish Reviews with prioritized backlog changes and clear owners so feedback results in concrete next steps.

screens.title: Sprint Retrospective: Inspect the Team and Improve
screens.subtitle: Create a plan for process improvements to enact in the next Sprint

narration.text: The Sprint Retrospective is the Scrum Team’s opportunity to inspect how they worked and plan concrete improvements for the next Sprint. Time-boxed to a maximum of three hours for a one-month Sprint (and shorter for shorter Sprints), the Retrospective asks the team three core questions: what went well, what could be improved, and what will we commit to improve next Sprint. The Scrum Master facilitates a positive, action-focused session that avoids blame. A crucial outcome is at least one high-priority, actionable improvement the team commits to implementing. For example, a team might commit to improving continuous integration tests by creating a checklist and assigning an owner. A common anti-pattern is holding a retrospective that surfaces problems but produces no concrete actions or owners. Fix this by converting insights into specific actions with owners and success criteria. Good retrospectives shorten feedback loops and steadily increase quality and team effectiveness over successive Sprints. Sprint Retrospective: Inspect the Team and Improve means retrospectives must end with a committed, high-priority action to improve the team’s process.. In practical terms, create a plan for process improvements to enact in the next sprint. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Inspect and commit
keyIdea.text: Retrospectives must end with a committed, high-priority action to improve the team’s process.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Sprint Retrospective
Purpose & Questions
  • Inspect team’s process and interactions.
  • Discuss what went well and what could improve.
  • Commit to one or more actionable improvements for the next Sprint.
Example action
Create a CI checklist and assign an owner to reduce broken builds, with success measured by reduced integration failures over the next Sprint.
Avoiding the blame game
Facilitate psychologically safe conversation. Convert concerns into experiments and actions rather than assigning fault. Ensure each action has an owner and measurable criteria.
Key Takeaway

Retrospectives drive continuous improvement when the team commits to concrete actions with owners and success criteria.

screens.title: Retrospective Anti-patterns and Action Planning
screens.subtitle: Turn observations into prioritized, owned actions

narration.text: Retrospectives can be powerful or a waste of time depending on follow-through. A common anti-pattern is raising many concerns without converting them into actions. Teams may leave feeling heard but unchanged. To avoid this, use a short action-planning step at the end: prioritize improvements, pick the top one or two, assign an owner, and define success criteria. Another anti-pattern is allowing the meeting to become a blame session. The Scrum Master must keep the tone constructive and focus on process changes rather than individual fault. A practical technique is to limit the number of improvement commitments to those the team can realistically try in the next Sprint, turning improvements into experiments. For example, if deployment took too long, the team might commit to automating one step and measure deployment time at the end of the next Sprint. This makes the Retrospective outcome concrete, measurable, and improvable over time. Which one improvement will your team commit to in the next Sprint? Retrospective Anti-patterns and Action Planning means prioritize a small number of improvements, assign owners, and define measurable success criteria before the sprint ends.. In practical terms, turn observations into prioritized, owned actions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: From observation to experiment
keyIdea.text: Prioritize a small number of improvements, assign owners, and define measurable success criteria before the Sprint ends.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Retrospective → Action
Common anti-patterns
Many observations, no actions or owners.
Blame-focused conversation that discourages openness.
Action planning recipe
  1. List potential improvements and vote to prioritize.
  2. Select one or two items the team can try next Sprint.
  3. Assign an owner and define measurable success criteria.
Key Takeaway

Limit commitments to achievable experiments, assign owners, and measure success at the end of the next Sprint.

screens.title: Event Flow Inside a Sprint
screens.subtitle: How Sprint Planning, Daily Scrums, Sprint Review, and Retrospective connect

narration.text: A Sprint is best understood as a short timeline with recurring, linked events. It begins with Sprint Planning, where the team sets a Sprint Goal and forms the Sprint Backlog. During the Sprint, the Development Team uses the Daily Scrum each day to inspect progress and plan the next 24 hours, adapting the Sprint Backlog as needed. Near the end of the Sprint the Sprint Review inspects the Increment with stakeholders and adapts the Product Backlog based on feedback. Finally, the Sprint Retrospective inspects the team and process and creates improvement commitments for the next Sprint. These events form a loop: planning creates the work, daily inspection keeps it on track, review brings external feedback, and retrospective improves the process that produces the next Increment. A practical two-week example: Planning on day one, Daily Scrums every workday, Review on the last workday for stakeholder feedback, and Retrospective immediately after the Review to capture learning while fresh. The discipline of these linked events increases transparency and lets the team adapt both product and process in short cycles. How will this flow change what your team inspects each day?

keyIdea.title: Linked cadence
keyIdea.text: Events form a repeating loop: Plan → Inspect daily → Review with stakeholders → Improve the process.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Sprint Timeline
Two-week Sprint timeline (illustrative)
Day 1 — Sprint Planning
Set Sprint Goal and Sprint Backlog. Time-box ~4 hours.
Days 2–9 — Daily Scrum
15 minutes each day to inspect progress and adapt plan.
Day 10 — Sprint Review
Demonstrate Increment and gather stakeholder feedback. Time-box ~2 hours.
Day 10 — Retrospective
Inspect process and commit to improvements. Time-box ~1.5 hours.
This rhythm forms a feedback loop: Planning sets the work, Daily Scrums keep it aligned, Reviews inform product direction, and Retrospectives improve team effectiveness for the next Sprint.

narration.text: These compact concept cards summarize the essential Scrum events and the Sprint container. First, the Sprint is a fixed time-box of one month or less during which a Done, usable Increment is created. Second, Sprint Planning is where the Scrum Team defines the Sprint Goal and selects Product Backlog items that the Development Team will commit to delivering, deciding how to accomplish that work. Third, the Daily Scrum is a 15-minute planning meeting for the Development Team to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog daily. Memorize these definitions and their time-boxes; they are the backbone of Scrum’s inspect-and-adapt rhythm. One quick tip: treat time-boxes as constraints that create learning and predictability rather than mere scheduling limits. When you apply these ideas, you’ll notice planning gets sharper, daily coordination improves, and the team’s delivery becomes more predictable.

keyIdea.title: Remember these terms
keyIdea.text: Sprint: container. Sprint Planning: define goal & backlog. Daily Scrum: daily planning for the team.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Key Concepts
Sprint
A time-box of one month or less for creating a Done Increment.
Sprint Planning
Event to set a Sprint Goal and select Product Backlog items for the Sprint.
Daily Scrum
Short 15-minute planning meeting for the Development Team to adapt daily.
Summary
These concepts create a disciplined cadence that enables regular inspection and adaptation of both product and process.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 2
screens.subtitle: Review of Review and Retrospective plus time-boxing

narration.text: Finish with the last core concepts. The Sprint Review is the working meeting where the Scrum Team and stakeholders inspect the Increment and adapt the Product Backlog. Reviews should be interactive, producing prioritized backlog updates rather than passive demos. The Sprint Retrospective is the team’s session to inspect its own process and commit to concrete improvements for the next Sprint; it must produce at least one actionable item with an owner and success criteria. Lastly, time-boxing is the discipline that bounds each event with a maximum duration. Time-boxes protect focus and create learning by forcing decisions and timely feedback. Remember: do not extend a Sprint to finish work; instead, return unfinished items to the Product Backlog and learn from planning and execution. Carry these concise definitions into your next Sprint plan and use them as checks when an event feels off-purpose.

keyIdea.title: Review, Retrospect, Time-box
keyIdea.text: Reviews inform the backlog, retrospectives inform process, and time-boxes create discipline and predictability.

For Sprint Retrospective, depict a team brainstorming improvements on a whiteboard. Emphasize the time-boxes visually with a countdown timer for each event. The tone should be hands-on and practical.
